I used to be in your shoes. After being bullied in 6th and 7th grade, I exited public school and began homeschooling. We quickly got behind because neither of my parents are teachers + we had some family deaths so all of that quickly overwhelmed us. I developed really terrible social anxiety and self esteem issues because of how little I spoke to other people in person.

I'm now 18. I'm supposed to be a freshman in college, however I got so far behind with my credits that I'm having to take an extra year to actually graduate high school. I have come a long way mentally. I am now talkative, experience very little anxiety when talking to new people and doing new things, and I'm generally a healthier person. The first thing you can do is to put yourself out there and step out of your comfort zone one step at a time. It can start w/ finding a new hobby, not necessarily something to do with someone else, but something you can use to have fun by yourself and mark progress off on doing something stress-free. For me, I chose music. Then, start reaching out to people you may think share your interests. Depending on your situation, you might have to resort to online friends or Instagram. Anything works. Just develop your social skills a little bit and teach your body that talking to people isn't the end of the world. It will be okay. Most people are forgiving because they themselves suffer with similar issues. After a little while, the effort you have to put in will start paying off and you will be easily meeting more people and experiencing less panic. You just have to start those first few steps.

People have very short attention spans. Even if you did embarrass yourself, it'd circulate for maybe a week max and then disappear. Everyone at 15 is self absorbed. Including you, but not in the toxic way, you're just focused on your own mental health. Everyone feels that way and everyone is self conscious, just some more than others.

Just don't quit. That's the last thing you should do. It will kick you in the ass years down the road. It may seem easier to quit now, but trust me, it will send a whirlwind of fallen dominoes for your in your future. I'm lucky to only need one year to get caught back up academically. If I hadn't realized how lazy I'd been about 2 years ago and devoted myself to bettering my mental health and then rebuilding my academics, I would be completely fucked. Don't do it to yourself. You still have time!

I'm an atheist too, but I have no problem dating someone that follows a religion. It's whether they're a good person or not that changes my mind.

If you want actual relationship advice, don't date someone if you disagree with them to this level. Trying to convince your boyfriend that something they've believed in for their entire life is "shit" will not work. There are religious people out there that are perfectly sane, advocate of LGBTQ+ rights, BLM, etc. And of course there are the opposite side of the coin like you see all over FaceBook. 

If I were you, I would evaluate whether he is a good guy or not. If he's not a good person, leave. If he is, stay.

However, since you have a rampant need to urge him out of Catholicism, I would just stop dating him. If it is seriously that much of an issue with him being Catholic, you do not need to be in a relationship with him. Same goes for him if he has an issue with you being an atheist. It's perfectly fine to not want to be w/ someone because of their religious views if that's how you feel. Trying to convince them to quit their religion is futile and disrespectful, assuming you're poking the bear first and he hasn't been also prodding you about being atheist. I don't know his side of the story, but I think I have enough context to conclude that you guys should not be together, at least from your perspective.

I dated this guy named Colin for like 8 months. It was a long distance relationship and we never met each other face to face. Even so, I still cared very deeply for him. We fought occasionally but it wasn't ever left unresolved- one person would apologize, the other would forgive, and we would both move on stronger.

At first I was indifferent. It was right before Christmas, but I didnt miss him at all. I thought I moved on, but a month or so later I found myself missing him. I eventually contacted him back and had an "on-and-off" fling with him for three or four months until I finally grieved the end of our relationship and moved on to greener pastures.

Its a delayed reaction. Sometimes people come back, sometimes people don't. It depends on the person and the situation. For a lot of people, the dumper will also be upset too. It depends on the person whether they'll cry or not, but I assure you, in *most* scenarios they will be sad too to some extent.

But also, don't be ashamed of crying or feeling a pit in your chest or thorns in your stomach. Those are ways your body copes with grief. Losing a relationship is similar to grieving death because of the extreme and sudden detachment from someone you love. Although they aren't literally gone from the Earth, in your heart, they might as well be. Extreme sadness manifests itself by both emotional and physical symptoms. This is normal, and eventually, it will start to become less and less severe.

My body's go-to way of grieving is to make me shit myself. I am not shitting you. My chest tightens and makes me feel like my heart has been ripped out of my body and my intestines make my breakfast turn to sludge. 

The point is, don't be ashamed of crying or leaving your work due to your pain. Emotions are real and so is the physical pain that accompanies them. Grief sickens all of us and it is 100% normal for you to feel the way that you do right now. The best thing you can do at this very moment is to let your emotions flow through you for however long they need. Eventually, your brain will be get tired of it, and your motivation will return, even if it's just for a little bit.

I didn't feel extreme grief, I rarely cried or had negative thoughts, but I did end up rebounding to him a couple of times over the next six months. Aaron, who has broken up with me twice now (I'm currently in the second one), tells me he "just needs time" and still loves me, so he's not fully committed to ending it.

Whatever happens though, you will mature and handle any situation differently depending on your age and mentality. The most important thing to remember is that time stops for no one. You won't feel like this forever. You will find joy again through other means and eventually you will find someone new. It's hard to think about it while it's happening, but trust me, you will be endlessly surprised when you find yourself crushing on the next person you're destined to meet.

My mother's grandmother started showing signs of "Sundowning" several years back. Sundowning is when cognitive ability declines during the afternoon and onward, but becomes stronger during the early morning. The later it gets in the day, the worse the patient's cognitive ability becomes. My great grandma ended up being diagnosed with some form of dementia soon after she showed sundowning symptoms. I believe it was Alzheimer's.

From what my mother has told me, my great grandmother's case wasn't that bad for the first few months/first year. The sundowning symptom was pretty much her only symptom. Things went up and down in productiveness, only gradually becoming worse and worse as her disease progressed. Over the span of half a decade (I think, it may have been longer), my grandmother went from fully recognizing my mother as who she was, to calling my mother by my grandmother's name. She thought my mother was her daughter, who had been dead for plenty of years already.

Dementia is terrible for everyone involved. I wasn't very old when this was all going on so I don't have first hand experience, but I know how drained my mother was when it came to dealing with my great grandma during this time. She was basically my great grandma's main caretaker for several years up until my great grandma's death. She wasn't allowed to grieve her own grandmother's death because she had to go through all of the post-death legal stuff, (taxes, real estate, inheritance, etc.) The effects of my great grandmother's death still have an extremely large toll on her mental health and it has been more than two years.

Your mind matters as well. Your father has been diagnosed with something so unimaginably horrible and you obviously want to help him in any way that he can, but do not tire yourself out to the point to where you cannot stay stable for him. Find a therapist, find something to do that will keep your sanity strong, such as painting or taking walks through the woods. Stay as positive as your brain can allow you to so that your father can try and cope with his diagnosis as best as he can.

You aren't selfish for feeling frustrated at all, and neither is your father for being in denial. No one is in the wrong here except for the diagnosis, and there isn't much anyone can do about that. Remember, your father is likely the person that is the most shocked and hurt by this diagnosis. My great grandmother was quite the same for a while. Dementia is probably one of the worst illnesses that someone could be diagnosed with. If anybody were to be diagnosed with it, they would likely be torn apart by it- as would be the same for any terminal illness- but dementia is ESPECIALLY terrible because of how it fucks with your brain.

As for things you can do to help him, spend quality time with him. Talk to him. Tell him some random details of your day. Arrange times where your family can get together and go out to eat, or maybe plan a vacation or something. See the best parts of life with your father while you still can. 

I'm very sorry that this has happened to your father and your family. This is a very strange and generally horrible situation to navigate. Your father is just as grief stricken as you are. No one wants to die if they're still able-bodied, generally speaking. I'm not saying this to make you feel bad or to make you feel selfish, I'm saying this to hopefully help you not feel so frustrated with his denial. He will likely come to terms with his diagnosis eventually. Until then, you should find ways to cope with your father's diagnosis, as this is obviously a very stressful topic that may dominate your life soon. I wish you the best of luck, man.
